course.title: HLSL Shader Programming for Unity
course.description: A comprehensive course taking you from shader basics to writing custom HLSL shaders in Unity. Covers the rendering pipeline, shader anatomy, properties, vertex/fragment shaders, lighting, textures, and a capstone project.

blocks.value: Welcome to the World of Shaders

A shader is a small program that runs on the GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) to determine how objects look on screen. Shaders control color, lighting, texture mapping, shadows, and visual effects. In Unity, shaders are written in HLSL (High-Level Shading Language) and define how every pixel of your game is rendered.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing CPU sends mesh data → GPU shader pipeline → final pixel on screen
blocks.caption: Shaders bridge 3D geometry data to the final pixels you see on screen

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Infographic/Diagram — A visual flowchart showing: '3D Model (Mesh + UVs)' → 'Vertex Shader' → 'Fragment/Pixel Shader' → 'Screen Pixels'. Use Unity's brand colors (dark gray, white, cyan accent). Show a before/after: flat gray cube vs lit, textured cube.
Why Learn HLSL Shaders?

• **Full creative control** — customize every visual aspect beyond what built-in materials offer
• **Performance** — hand-written shaders can be faster than Shader Graph for complex effects
• **Portability** — HLSL works across Unity's Built-in, URP, and HDRP pipelines
• **Industry standard** — HLSL knowledge transfers to Unreal, Godot, and custom engines
• **Career value** — shader programmers are highly sought after in game development

blocks.alt: Grid of shader effects: water, fire, hologram, toon shading, dissolve, outline
blocks.caption: Shaders create everything from water surfaces to holographic UI effects

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Showcase Grid — 2x3 grid showing diverse shader effects in Unity. Top row: stylized water with foam, cartoon toon shading, fire particle shader. Bottom row: holographic scanlines, dissolve effect, edge outline. Each with a small label. Use vibrant, game-ready visuals.
How Shaders Run on the GPU

The GPU processes thousands of shader instances in parallel. First, the **vertex shader** transforms 3D mesh vertices into screen space. Then, the **fragment shader** (also called pixel shader) calculates the final color for each pixel. This pipeline happens for every frame, 60+ times per second.

blocks.output: A solid red square/cube on screen

blocks.question: What is the primary role of a shader?
options: To determine how objects look on screen
blocks.correctAnswer: To determine how objects look on screen
blocks.explanation: Shaders are GPU programs that calculate color, lighting, and visual effects for every pixel rendered on screen.

blocks.question: Which of the following is NOT a reason to learn HLSL shaders?
options: Shaders handle game logic and AI
blocks.correctAnswer: Shaders handle game logic and AI
blocks.explanation: Shaders run on the GPU and only handle visual rendering. Game logic and AI are handled by C# scripts running on the CPU.

blocks.question: What language are Unity shaders primarily written in?
blocks.explanation: Unity shaders use HLSL (High-Level Shading Language), which is Microsoft's shading language adapted for Unity's rendering pipelines.

blocks.value: Understanding Unity's Rendering Pipeline

Unity supports three rendering pipelines: **Built-in RP** (legacy, still widely used), **URP** (Universal Render Pipeline — recommended for most projects), and **HDRP** (High Definition Render Pipeline — for high-end PC/console). This course focuses on URP as it's the modern standard for cross-platform development.

blocks.alt: Comparison of Built-in RP vs URP vs HDRP showing visual quality and platform targets
blocks.caption: URP is the recommended pipeline for learning shaders — it balances quality and performance

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Comparison Chart — Three columns side by side. Column 1: 'Built-in RP' with older visuals, label 'Legacy'. Column 2: 'URP' with modern clean visuals, label 'Recommended' with green checkmark. Column 3: 'HDRP' with photorealistic visuals, label 'High-end PC/Console'. Include platform icons (mobile, PC, console) under each.
Setting Up Your Shader Project

1. Create a new Unity 2022.3 LTS project with URP template
2. In Project window, right-click → Create → Shader → Unlit Shader (or HLSL Shader)
3. Create a Material and assign your shader to it
4. Apply the material to a 3D object (Cube, Sphere, or Plane)
5. Open the shader file in your code editor (Visual Studio or VS Code)

blocks.alt: Unity editor screenshot showing Project window with shader file, material, and Inspector panel
blocks.caption: The Unity workflow: create shader → create material → assign to mesh

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot — Unity editor with dark theme. Left: Project window showing 'MyFirstShader.shader' highlighted. Middle: Scene view with a cube using the shader. Right: Inspector showing Material properties. Use annotations/arrows to show the workflow path.

blocks.output: A solid-colored cube using the _Color property from the Material Inspector

blocks.value: Shader File Anatomy

Every Unity shader has these key sections:
1. **Shader declaration** — `Shader "Category/Name"` (defines the menu path)
2. **Properties** — variables exposed to the Material Inspector
3. **SubShader** — contains one or more Passes
4. **Pass** — a single rendering step (vertex + fragment stages)
5. **HLSLPROGRAM** — the actual shader code block

blocks.question: Which Unity render pipeline is recommended for most projects and this course?
blocks.explanation: URP is Unity's modern, cross-platform pipeline that balances quality and performance. It's the recommended default for new projects.

blocks.question: What section of a shader exposes variables to the Unity Material Inspector?
blocks.explanation: The Properties block defines shader variables that artists can tweak in the Material Inspector without editing code.

blocks.question: What keyword marks the start of the actual HLSL shader code block in Unity?
blocks.explanation: HLSLPROGRAM (and its closing ENDHLSL) wraps the actual shader code, including vertex and fragment functions.

blocks.value: Exposing Data with Properties

Properties are the bridge between your shader code and Unity's Material Inspector. They let artists and designers tweak colors, textures, numbers, and toggles without touching code. In HLSL, you must also declare a matching variable inside the shader program.

blocks.alt: Unity Inspector panel showing shader properties: Color picker, slider, texture slot, toggle
blocks.caption: Properties turn shader values into artist-friendly controls in the Inspector

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot/Diagram — Unity Inspector panel showing various property types. Top: Color property with color picker. Middle: Range property with slider (0-1). Bottom: 2D texture property with texture slot. Right side: matching HLSL variable declarations. Use annotations to link each UI control to its code counterpart.

blocks.output: Material Inspector shows color picker, brightness slider, texture slot, and toggle

blocks.value: HLSL Data Types

HLSL has specific data types optimized for GPU math:
• **`float`** — 32-bit precision, use for world positions and UVs
• **`half`** — 16-bit precision, use for colors and normals (faster)
• **`fixed`** — 12-bit precision, legacy, rarely used in URP
• **`int`** — whole numbers, use for array indices and toggles
• **`bool`** — true/false values
Common Property Types
Unity supports many property types for the Inspector. Here are the most common ones with their HLSL counterparts.
Property Attributes for Better UX
Unity provides attributes to customize how properties appear in the Inspector. These improve the artist experience significantly.

blocks.output: Inspector shows organized sections with headers, toggles, dropdowns, and HDR color picker

blocks.question: Which HLSL data type is best for storing colors in URP shaders?
blocks.explanation: half4 provides 16-bit precision which is sufficient for colors and runs faster on mobile GPUs. float4 is overkill for most color data.

blocks.question: What happens if you declare a Property but forget to declare the matching HLSL variable?
options: The shader compiles but shows pink
The property uses a default value silently
blocks.correctAnswer: The shader compiles but shows pink
blocks.explanation: Unity shows a magenta/pink color when a shader fails to compile or has missing variable bindings. Always declare matching HLSL variables.

blocks.question: What suffix is added to a texture property name for its tiling and offset data?
blocks.explanation: For a texture named _MainTex, Unity automatically provides _MainTex_ST which contains tiling (xy) and offset (zw) values.

blocks.value: The Vertex Shader Stage

The vertex shader is the first programmable stage in the rendering pipeline. It processes each vertex of your 3D mesh individually. Its main job is to transform vertex positions from **object space** (local to the model) to **clip space** (ready for the screen). But it can also pass data like UVs, normals, and colors to the fragment shader.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing coordinate spaces: Object → World → View → Clip → Screen
blocks.caption: The vertex shader transforms coordinates through multiple spaces to reach the screen

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A horizontal pipeline showing 5 coordinate spaces with arrows between them. Object (local mesh) → World (scene coordinates) → View (camera-relative) → Clip (normalized device) → Screen (final pixels). Each space has a small 3D axis icon. Highlight the vertex shader's role in the first three transformations. Use a 3D cube that morphs through each stage.

blocks.output: Mesh renders correctly with UVs and normals available in fragment stage

blocks.value: Coordinate Space Transformations
Unity's Shader Library provides helper functions for common transformations. Understanding these spaces is essential for advanced effects.
Vertex Displacement Effects

One of the most powerful vertex shader techniques is **vertex displacement** — modifying vertex positions before they reach the screen. This creates effects like waves, pulsing, and vertex animation without changing the mesh.

blocks.alt: Before/after comparison: flat plane vs wave-displaced plane using sine function in vertex shader
blocks.caption: Vertex displacement turns a flat plane into an animated wave surface

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Before/After Split — Left: flat gray plane grid. Right: same plane with sine wave displacement, showing peaks and valleys. Both with wireframe overlay to show vertex movement. Include the sine wave formula as an overlay annotation. Use a blue water-like color scheme.

blocks.output: Plane mesh animates up and down in a sine wave pattern

blocks.value: Semantics: What the Colons Mean

The colon syntax (`: POSITION`, `: TEXCOORD0`, `: SV_POSITION`) are called **semantics**. They tell the GPU what each variable represents. `SV_POSITION` is special — it means 'System Value Position' and is required for the vertex shader output.

blocks.question: What is the main job of the vertex shader?
options: To calculate the final pixel color
To transform vertex positions to clip space
blocks.correctAnswer: To transform vertex positions to clip space
blocks.explanation: The vertex shader's primary responsibility is transforming 3D vertex positions into clip space (screen-ready coordinates). Pixel color is handled by the fragment shader.

blocks.question: Which semantic is REQUIRED in the vertex shader output struct?
blocks.explanation: SV_POSITION (System Value Position) is mandatory. It tells the GPU where to place the vertex on screen. Without it, the shader won't compile.

blocks.question: What Unity function transforms object-space position directly to clip space?
blocks.explanation: TransformObjectToHClip is the URP helper function that converts local mesh coordinates directly to homogeneous clip space in one step.

blocks.value: The Fragment (Pixel) Shader Stage

The fragment shader (also called pixel shader) runs for every pixel that covers your mesh on screen. It receives interpolated data from the vertex shader — positions, UVs, normals — and outputs the final color. This is where lighting, texturing, and special effects happen.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing triangle rasterization: vertices → interpolated pixels → fragment shader colors each pixel
blocks.caption: The fragment shader colors every pixel that covers your mesh on screen

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A 3D triangle in clip space being rasterized into a grid of pixels. Show three vertices (red, green, blue) with arrows pointing to interpolated pixel colors inside the triangle. Label 'Vertex Shader' at vertices, 'Fragment Shader' at interior pixels. Use a gradient fill to show interpolation.

blocks.output: A solid-colored object using the _Color property

blocks.value: Sampling Textures
The most common fragment shader operation is texture sampling — reading pixel colors from an image and applying them to your mesh. Use `SAMPLE_TEXTURE2D` in URP for proper platform support.

blocks.alt: Visual showing UV coordinates (0,0 to 1,1) mapping to a texture, then applied to a 3D cube
blocks.caption: UV coordinates map 2D texture pixels to 3D mesh surfaces

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Left: a 2D texture with a grid showing UV coordinates (0,0 at bottom-left, 1,1 at top-right). Middle: arrows showing how UVs wrap around a 3D cube. Right: the final textured cube. Use a checkerboard texture for clarity. Include small UV coordinate labels on the cube faces.

blocks.output: Object displays the assigned texture, tinted by the _Color property

blocks.value: UV Manipulation Effects
By manipulating UV coordinates in the fragment shader, you can create scrolling textures, distortion, and animated effects without changing the mesh.

blocks.output: Texture appears to scroll or warp based on the effect applied

blocks.value: Alpha and Transparency
To make objects transparent, you need three things: an alpha channel in your color, the correct blend mode, and the right render queue. Unity's default opaque shaders ignore alpha.

blocks.output: Object renders with adjustable transparency

blocks.question: Which shader stage determines the final color of each pixel?
blocks.explanation: The fragment (pixel) shader runs once per pixel and outputs the final RGBA color that appears on screen.

blocks.question: What URP macro applies tiling and offset to UV coordinates?
blocks.explanation: TRANSFORM_TEX(uv, textureName) applies the texture's tiling (xy) and offset (zw) values stored in textureName_ST.

blocks.question: What built-in HLSL variable provides elapsed time for animations?
blocks.explanation: _Time is a built-in float4 where _Time.y gives elapsed time in seconds. It's essential for creating animated shader effects.

blocks.value: Understanding Light in Shaders

Lighting is what transforms flat, colored shapes into believable 3D objects. In shaders, lighting calculations determine how bright each pixel should be based on the light source direction, surface normal, and view angle. The two most fundamental lighting models are **Lambert (diffuse)** and **Blinn-Phong (specular)**.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing light ray hitting surface: diffuse reflection scatters, specular reflects at angle
blocks.caption: Diffuse light scatters in all directions; specular light reflects at a mirror angle

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A 3D surface with a light ray hitting it from the top-left. Show two reflection paths: 1) Diffuse — multiple arrows scattering in all directions from the impact point (matte look). 2) Specular — a single sharp reflection arrow at the mirror angle (shiny highlight). Label 'Normal' as a perpendicular line from the surface. Use warm yellow for light, cool blue for surface.
The Dot Product: Lighting's Secret Weapon

The dot product is the mathematical heart of lighting. It measures how aligned two vectors are. When the surface normal faces the light, the dot product is 1 (full brightness). When perpendicular, it's 0 (no light). When facing away, it's negative (we clamp to 0).

blocks.output: Surface is bright where facing light, dark where facing away

blocks.value: URP's Built-in Lighting Helpers

URP provides powerful built-in functions and variables for lighting. Instead of calculating everything from scratch, you can use Unity's optimized lighting pipeline. The key include is `Lighting.hlsl` which gives you `GetMainLight()`, `LightingLambert()`, and more.

blocks.output: Lit surface with directional light, shadow support, and proper attenuation

blocks.value: Ambient Light and Global Illumination

Real scenes aren't just lit by direct light — ambient light fills shadowed areas. URP provides `SampleSH()` for spherical harmonics (cheap ambient) and you can add a simple ambient term for basic fill lighting.

blocks.output: Surface with both direct lighting and soft ambient fill in shadows

blocks.value: Specular Highlights (Blinn-Phong)

Specular highlights create the shiny 'hotspot' you see on polished surfaces. Blinn-Phong uses the **halfway vector** (between light direction and view direction) instead of the pure reflection vector — it's cheaper and looks great.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing Blinn-Phong specular: light vector + view vector = halfway vector, dot with normal
blocks.caption: Blinn-Phong specular uses the halfway vector for efficient shiny highlights

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — A 3D surface with three vectors: Light direction (L, yellow arrow from surface to light), View direction (V, blue arrow from surface to camera), and Halfway vector (H, green arrow — the normalized sum of L and V). Show the Normal (N, perpendicular line). The specular highlight intensity is determined by dot(N, H) raised to a power. Include a small sphere showing the resulting highlight.

blocks.output: Surface with diffuse base, ambient fill, and sharp specular highlight

blocks.question: What mathematical operation is the core of diffuse lighting calculations?
blocks.explanation: The dot product between the surface normal and light direction gives the cosine of the angle between them — exactly what we need for diffuse brightness.

blocks.question: What URP function retrieves the main directional light data?
blocks.explanation: GetMainLight() returns a Light struct containing color, direction, distance attenuation, and shadow attenuation for the scene's main directional light.

blocks.question: What HLSL function clamps a value between 0 and 1?
blocks.explanation: saturate(x) is the GPU-optimized way to clamp values to [0, 1]. It's faster than max(0, min(1, x)) on most hardware.

blocks.value: Adding Surface Detail with Normal Maps

Normal maps are textures that store surface direction (normal vectors) instead of color. They let you fake complex surface details — bumps, grooves, scratches — without adding extra geometry. A flat plane with a good normal map can look like rough stone or woven fabric.

blocks.alt: Before/after: flat cube with color texture vs same cube with normal map showing fake surface bumps
blocks.caption: Normal maps fake surface detail without adding a single extra polygon

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Before/After Split — Left: a flat cube with just a brick color texture — looks like a flat painting. Right: same cube with a normal map applied — the surface appears to have real depth, mortar grooves, and roughness. Both with identical geometry (show wireframe overlay). Label 'Same mesh, different normals'. Use a brick wall texture as the example.
How Normal Maps Work

A normal map stores XYZ normal components in the RGB channels of a texture. The default 'flat' normal is (0, 0, 1) which maps to the color (128, 128, 255) — the distinctive blue-purple color of most normal maps. When sampled, these values are unpacked from [0,1] color space to [-1,1] vector space.

blocks.output: Surface shows fake bumps and grooves based on the normal map texture

blocks.value: Tangent Space vs World Space

Normal maps store vectors in **tangent space** — relative to the surface's UV orientation. To use them for lighting, you must transform them to **world space** where your light vectors live. This requires the **TBN matrix** (Tangent, Bitangent, Normal).

blocks.alt: Diagram showing TBN basis vectors: Tangent along U, Bitangent along V, Normal perpendicular
blocks.caption: The TBN matrix transforms tangent-space normals to world space for lighting

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: 3D Diagram — A 3D surface patch with three orthogonal arrows: Tangent (T, red, along U direction), Bitangent/Binormal (B, green, along V direction), Normal (N, blue, perpendicular). Show a small normal vector in tangent space being transformed by the TBN matrix to world space. Label 'Tangent Space' and 'World Space'. Use a coordinate system visual with clear axis colors.

blocks.output: Lit surface with normal map bumps affecting the lighting direction

blocks.value: Object-Space Normal Maps (Alternative)

Some assets use **object-space** normal maps (sometimes called 'world-space' normal maps). These store normals directly in object space — no TBN matrix needed! They're great for static objects but don't work well with animated/deformed meshes since the normals are baked to a specific orientation.

blocks.output: Object-space normal map applied without TBN matrix calculation

blocks.value: Common Normal Map Mistakes

Beginners often make these normal map mistakes:
• **Forgetting to normalize** — always call `normalize()` on your final normal
• **Wrong space** — mixing tangent-space normal with world-space light direction
• **Strength too high** — values above 1 create physically impossible normals
• **Not reconstructing Z** — if you scale XY, you must recalculate Z to keep the vector unit-length
• **Import settings** — Unity must know a texture is a normal map (set Texture Type to 'Normal Map')

blocks.question: What color represents a 'flat' normal in a tangent-space normal map?
blocks.explanation: A flat normal pointing straight out is (0, 0, 1) in [-1,1] space, which maps to (128, 128, 255) in [0,1] texture space — the characteristic blue-purple color.

blocks.question: What does TBN stand for in normal mapping?
blocks.explanation: TBN is the basis matrix: Tangent (along U), Bitangent (along V), and Normal (perpendicular). It transforms tangent-space normals to world space.

blocks.question: What URP function unpacks a normal map texture from [0,1] to [-1,1]?
blocks.explanation: UnpackNormal() converts normal map texture data from the 0-1 color range to the -1 to 1 vector range that HLSL expects for normal calculations.

blocks.value: Beyond Realistic: Stylized Lighting

Not every game wants photorealism. Stylized shaders — cel-shading, toon lighting, rim lighting — are essential for games like Zelda, Genshin Impact, and Fortnite. These effects often require **custom lighting functions** that replace Unity's default realistic calculations with artist-controlled steps.

blocks.alt: Comparison: smooth realistic shading vs stepped cel-shading with sharp light/dark bands
blocks.caption: Cel-shading replaces smooth gradients with discrete color bands for a cartoon look

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Before/After Split — Left: a sphere with smooth Blinn-Phong lighting showing gradual light-to-dark transition. Right: same sphere with cel-shading — 3-4 distinct color bands (bright highlight, mid-tone, shadow, deep shadow) with sharp boundaries between them. Label 'Realistic' vs 'Cel-Shaded (Toon)'. Use a vibrant, anime-inspired color palette for the toon version.
Cel-Shading with Step Functions

The core of cel-shading is quantizing (rounding) the lighting value into discrete steps. Instead of smooth NdotL values from 0 to 1, we create 3-4 distinct bands. The `smoothstep` function creates soft transitions between bands to avoid harsh aliasing.

blocks.output: Sphere with 3 distinct lighting bands: shadow, mid-tone, and highlight

blocks.value: Rim Lighting for Character Highlights

Rim lighting adds a bright edge glow where the surface faces away from the camera. It's iconic in anime, sci-fi, and character art. The effect uses the dot product between the normal and view direction — when they face opposite directions (perpendicular to camera), the rim is strongest.

blocks.alt: Character model showing rim light effect: bright cyan edge glow on silhouette edges
blocks.caption: Rim lighting creates a glowing edge that makes characters pop from the background

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Character Render — A 3D character (anime-style or sci-fi) against a dark background. Show a bright rim light (cyan or warm orange) tracing the silhouette edges — shoulders, head outline, arm edges. Include a small inset diagram showing: Normal vector (perpendicular to surface) and View vector (to camera). The rim intensity = 1 - dot(N, V). Label 'Rim = 1 - N·V'. Use dramatic lighting with the rim as the focal point.

blocks.output: Object shows bright edge glow on silhouette-facing surfaces

blocks.value: Outline Effects with Inverted Hull

A classic toon technique is the **inverted hull outline**: render the mesh a second time, flip the normals inward, and push vertices outward along those inverted normals. This creates a solid-colored shell around the object that looks like an outline.

blocks.output: Object renders with a solid colored outline around its silhouette

blocks.value: Custom Lighting Functions
For complex stylized looks, you'll want to write your own lighting function instead of using Unity's built-in Lambert. This gives you complete control over how light interacts with your surface.

blocks.output: Fully custom toon shader with stepped lighting and rim highlight

blocks.question: What function creates smooth transitions between cel-shading bands?
blocks.explanation: smoothstep(min, max, x) returns a smooth Hermite interpolation between 0 and 1, creating soft band edges instead of harsh aliased lines.

blocks.question: What does the inverted hull outline technique do?
options: Draws lines using a geometry shader
Renders backfaces pushed outward along normals
Uses a post-processing edge detection filter
Adds a second texture with black borders
blocks.correctAnswer: Renders backfaces pushed outward along normals
blocks.explanation: The inverted hull method renders the mesh again with Cull Front, pushing vertices along their inverted normals to create a shell that appears as an outline.

blocks.question: What value is rim lighting based on? (1 minus what dot product?)
blocks.explanation: Rim lighting uses 1 - dot(Normal, ViewDirection). When the surface faces away from the camera, NdotV approaches 0, making the rim term approach 1 (full brightness).

parts.partTitle: Part 9: Shader Graph vs Hand-Written HLSL

blocks.value: When to Use Shader Graph vs HLSL

Unity's Shader Graph is a powerful visual node-based shader editor. It lets you create shaders without writing code by connecting nodes in a graph. But hand-written HLSL still has important advantages. Knowing both workflows makes you a more versatile technical artist or graphics programmer.

blocks.alt: Side-by-side: Shader Graph node network vs HLSL code editor showing equivalent shader
blocks.caption: The same shader effect can be built visually in Shader Graph or written as HLSL code

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Split Screen Comparison — Left: Unity Shader Graph interface showing a node network (Sample Texture 2D → Multiply → Fragment). Nodes are colorful boxes with connection wires. Right: VS Code showing the equivalent HLSL code with syntax highlighting. Both produce the same result (textured, tinted object). Label 'Visual' vs 'Code'. Include a small 'equals' sign between them.
Shader Graph Strengths

• **Visual prototyping** — iterate on effects rapidly without compile times
• **Artist-friendly** — technical artists can create shaders without programming
• **Live preview** — see changes instantly in the Graph Inspector
• **Built-in nodes** — common operations like Fresnel, Noise, and Remap are pre-built
• **Easier debugging** — visual flow makes it obvious where data comes from
Hand-Written HLSL Strengths

• **Performance control** — write exactly the instructions the GPU executes, no bloat
• **Advanced features** — custom vertex streams, multiple passes, compute shaders
• **Version control** — text files diff beautifully; graph files are binary/JSON blobs
• **Reusability** — #include files let you share code across many shaders
• **Debugging** — shader compilers give precise error line numbers
• **Portability** — HLSL knowledge transfers to Unreal, Godot, and custom engines
Hybrid Workflow: Best of Both Worlds

Many professional workflows combine both approaches: prototype in Shader Graph for speed, then convert to HLSL for optimization and advanced features. Unity even lets you create **Custom Function nodes** in Shader Graph that call your own HLSL code.

blocks.alt: Shader Graph showing a Custom Function node connected to the graph, calling external HLSL file
blocks.caption: Custom Function nodes let you inject hand-written HLSL into Shader Graph workflows

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot — Unity Shader Graph with a 'Custom Function' node highlighted. The node has input/output ports and a file reference to 'MyCustomLighting.hlsl'. Show wires connecting from a Texture node → Custom Function → Fragment Color. Include a small code preview popup showing the HLSL function inside the node. Use Unity's dark theme.

blocks.output: Shader Graph node calls your custom HLSL cel-shading function

blocks.value: Converting Shader Graph to HLSL

To learn from Shader Graph, you can inspect the generated HLSL. In Shader Graph, go to the **Compile Code** button (or check the generated code in the Inspector). This shows you exactly what nodes translate to — an excellent learning tool!

blocks.question: Which is NOT an advantage of hand-written HLSL over Shader Graph?
options: Better version control with text diffs
blocks.explanation: Instant visual preview is actually Shader Graph's advantage! HLSL requires compilation and scene refresh to see changes. The other options are genuine HLSL strengths.

blocks.question: What Shader Graph feature lets you inject hand-written HLSL code?
blocks.explanation: The Custom Function node references an external HLSL file and exposes its inputs/outputs as graph nodes, bridging visual and code workflows.

blocks.question: What pragma directive creates shader keyword variants for different features?
blocks.explanation: #pragma multi_compile generates multiple shader variants at build time. Unity selects the correct variant at runtime based on active keywords (like _MAIN_LIGHT_SHADOWS).

blocks.value: Writing GPU-Friendly Shaders

A beautiful shader that runs at 15 FPS is useless. GPU optimization is about understanding what makes the graphics card work hard — texture samples, complex math, branching, and overdraw — then minimizing those costs. This part covers the techniques that separate production-ready shaders from hobby experiments.

blocks.alt: Performance comparison chart: unoptimized shader vs optimized shader showing FPS and GPU time
blocks.caption: Optimized shaders can run 5-10x faster while looking nearly identical

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Bar Chart — Two bars side by side. Left (red): 'Unoptimized Shader' — 12 FPS, 8.3ms GPU time, 45 texture samples, 200 instructions. Right (green): 'Optimized Shader' — 60 FPS, 1.6ms GPU time, 4 texture samples, 45 instructions. Show a small arrow with '5x faster' label. Include a tiny before/after render showing they look identical. Use performance dashboard styling.
Minimize Texture Samples

Texture sampling (`SAMPLE_TEXTURE2D`) is one of the most expensive operations in a fragment shader. Each sample reads from GPU memory, which is slow. Aim for 1-4 texture samples per shader. If you need multiple textures, consider packing them into channels of a single texture (e.g., roughness in R, metallic in G, occlusion in B).
Avoid Dynamic Branching

GPUs execute shaders in lockstep across many pixels simultaneously. When pixels take different code paths (if/else branches), the GPU must execute BOTH paths and mask out the wrong results — doubling the work. Use `lerp`, `step`, and `saturate` instead of conditionals when possible.
Use Appropriate Precision

Not every calculation needs 32-bit float precision. On mobile GPUs especially, using `half` (16-bit) instead of `float` (32-bit) can double your arithmetic throughput. Use `half` for colors, UVs, and normalized vectors. Use `float` only for world positions and depth calculations.
Shader LOD and Fallbacks

Unity's **Shader LOD** system lets you specify quality levels. Lower-end devices automatically use simpler shader variants. Always provide a fallback so your object doesn't render as magenta if the shader fails.

blocks.output: Shader automatically selects appropriate quality based on device capabilities

blocks.value: Profiling Shaders in Unity

Unity provides several tools to measure shader performance:
• **Frame Debugger** (Window → Analysis → Frame Debugger) — step through draw calls
• **Profiler** (Window → Analysis → Profiler) — GPU time per shader
• **Rendering Statistics** (Game view Stats overlay) — draw calls, tris, texture memory
• **Shader Complexity view** — some platforms show estimated instruction count
The Optimization Checklist

Before shipping any shader, run through this checklist:
• [ ] Texture samples minimized and packed where possible
• [ ] No dynamic branching in fragment shaders
• [ ] Appropriate precision (half vs float) throughout
• [ ] Shader LOD and fallback configured
• [ ] ZWrite correct for transparency mode
• [ ] Cull mode appropriate (Cull Back for solid, Cull Off for double-sided)
• [ ] Tested on target hardware (especially mobile!)
• [ ] Frame Debugger shows expected number of draw calls

blocks.question: What is the most expensive operation to minimize in fragment shaders?
blocks.explanation: Texture sampling reads from GPU memory, which is significantly slower than arithmetic operations. Minimizing samples (aim for 1-4) is the #1 optimization for fragment shaders.

blocks.question: Why should you avoid if/else branching in fragment shaders?
options: GPUs execute both paths and mask results
It makes code harder to read
blocks.correctAnswer: GPUs execute both paths and mask results
blocks.explanation: GPUs process pixels in lockstep groups (warps/wavefronts). When pixels branch differently, the GPU executes BOTH branches and discards the wrong results, effectively doubling the work.

blocks.question: What HLSL data type should you use for colors and normalized vectors on mobile?
blocks.explanation: half provides 16-bit precision which is sufficient for colors (0-1 range) and normalized vectors. On mobile GPUs, half arithmetic is often 2x faster than float and uses half the register space.

blocks.value: Beyond Basic Texture Sampling

Once you master basic texture sampling, you can create powerful visual effects by manipulating UV coordinates, blending multiple textures, and using texture masks. These techniques are the foundation of terrain shaders, animated effects, and advanced material systems.

blocks.alt: Visual showing texture blending: base rock texture + moss overlay using a mask texture
blocks.caption: Texture masking lets you blend multiple materials based on a control texture

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Three panels side by side. Panel 1: 'Base Texture' showing gray rock. Panel 2: 'Mask Texture' showing a grayscale gradient (white at bottom, black at top). Panel 3: 'Blended Result' showing rock at top transitioning to green moss at bottom. Include arrows showing the blend formula: lerp(rock, moss, mask). Use a terrain/cliff visual as the example.
Texture Blending with Masks

Mask textures (also called splat maps or blend maps) use grayscale values to control how much of each texture appears at a given pixel. White = full secondary texture, black = full primary texture, gray = blend between them. This is essential for terrain shaders and complex materials.

blocks.output: Object shows smooth blend between two textures controlled by the mask

blocks.value: Triplanar Mapping for Seamless Surfaces

Triplanar mapping projects a texture from three axes (X, Y, Z) and blends them based on the surface normal. This eliminates UV stretching on steep surfaces and creates seamless textures on complex geometry without unwrapping — perfect for terrain, rocks, and procedural objects.

blocks.alt: Triplanar mapping visualization: three axis projections blended by normal direction on a sphere
blocks.caption: Triplanar mapping projects textures from X, Y, and Z axes and blends by surface normal

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: 3D Diagram — A sphere or cube showing three texture projections: red-tinted from X-axis, green-tinted from Y-axis, blue-tinted from Z-axis. Where faces are flat against an axis, that color dominates. At edges, colors blend smoothly. Include small axis arrows (X, Y, Z) and normal vectors showing how blending weights are calculated. Use a grid texture for clarity.

blocks.output: Seamless texture on any geometry without UV unwrapping

blocks.value: Texture Atlasing and Sprite Sheets

A texture atlas packs multiple images into one texture to reduce draw calls. Sprite sheets use the same technique for animation. You calculate UV offsets to select the correct sub-region of the atlas.

blocks.output: Animated sprite playing frames from a texture atlas

blocks.value: Parallax Mapping for Fake Depth

Parallax mapping offsets UV coordinates based on the view angle and a height map, creating the illusion of depth on a flat surface. It's cheaper than actual geometry displacement but looks convincing for moderate depth variations.

blocks.output: Surface appears to have physical depth when viewed from angles

blocks.question: What technique projects textures from three axes and blends by normal?
blocks.explanation: Triplanar mapping samples textures from X, Y, and Z axes and blends them using the surface normal direction, eliminating UV stretching on complex geometry.

blocks.question: What does a texture mask control in multi-texture blending?
options: The blend ratio between textures per pixel
The color tint of the material
blocks.correctAnswer: The blend ratio between textures per pixel
blocks.explanation: A mask texture's grayscale values control how much of each source texture appears at each pixel — white = full overlay, black = full base, gray = blend.

blocks.question: What HLSL function linearly interpolates between two values based on a blend factor?
blocks.explanation: lerp(a, b, t) returns a when t=0, b when t=1, and a linear blend between them for values in between. It's the GPU-friendly replacement for if/else blending.

blocks.value: Reading the Depth Buffer

Screen-space shaders read data from buffers that Unity renders before your shader runs — the color buffer, depth buffer, and normal buffer. This enables effects like fog, outlines, water depth, soft particles, and intersection glow that react to the entire scene, not just the current object.

blocks.alt: Visual showing depth buffer as grayscale image and screen-space intersection glow effect
blocks.caption: The depth buffer stores how far each pixel is from the camera — essential for screen-space effects

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Split Screen — Left: a 3D scene with a sphere partially inside a cube, both with a glowing intersection line. Right: the same scene's depth buffer shown as a grayscale image (white = near, black = far). Include a small depth gradient legend. Label 'Scene View' and 'Depth Buffer'. Use a sci-fi glow effect for the intersection.
Accessing Scene Depth in URP

URP provides the `_CameraDepthTexture` which contains the depth of every pixel from the camera's perspective. You sample it using screen-space UV coordinates to get the depth of geometry behind your object, then compare it with your object's depth.

blocks.output: Grayscale visualization of depth difference between object and scene behind it

blocks.value: Intersection Glow Effect

A popular screen-space effect is intersection glow — objects glow brighter where they intersect with other geometry. This is used for force fields, magical barriers, sci-fi shields, and water foam lines.

blocks.alt: Force field sphere showing bright cyan glow only where it intersects with floor and walls
blocks.caption: Intersection glow creates a bright edge wherever your object meets other geometry

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot — A translucent cyan force field sphere in a sci-fi room. The sphere is mostly transparent, but where it touches the floor and walls, there's a bright glowing edge (like an energy barrier). Show a small inset with the depth-difference math visualization. Use a dark environment with neon cyan glow for dramatic effect.

blocks.output: Transparent object with bright glow at geometry intersections

blocks.value: Soft Particles with Depth Fade

Hard-edged particles clipping into geometry looks terrible. By reading the depth buffer, you can fade particles out as they approach solid surfaces — creating soft, natural-looking smoke, fire, and magic effects.

blocks.output: Particles softly fade out instead of clipping into solid geometry

blocks.value: Screen-Space UV Distortion

You can distort the screen UVs before sampling the scene color to create heat haze, underwater refraction, and glass distortion effects. This requires the `_CameraOpaqueTexture` which contains the rendered scene color.

blocks.output: Scene appears distorted/wavy like heat haze or underwater

blocks.question: What URP texture contains the depth of every pixel from the camera?
blocks.explanation: _CameraDepthTexture is automatically populated by URP when enabled in the Renderer settings. It stores per-pixel depth values for screen-space effects.

blocks.question: What function converts raw depth buffer values to linear eye-space depth?
blocks.explanation: LinearEyeDepth(rawDepth, _ZBufferParams) converts the non-linear depth buffer value to actual world-unit distance from the camera. Linear01Depth gives 0-1 range instead.

blocks.question: What include file provides the SampleSceneDepth function in URP?
blocks.explanation: #include "Packages/com.unity.render-pipelines.universal/ShaderLibrary/DeclareDepthTexture.hlsl" gives you access to SampleSceneDepth() and the _CameraDepthTexture.

blocks.value: GPU Computing Beyond Rendering

Compute shaders are GPU programs that don't render pixels at all. Instead, they run general-purpose calculations on thousands of threads in parallel — perfect for particle systems, fluid simulation, procedural generation, and post-processing. They're the bridge between graphics programming and GPU-accelerated computing.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing CPU sends compute dispatch → GPU runs thousands of threads in parallel → results written to buffer/texture
blocks.caption: Compute shaders run parallel calculations on the GPU without rendering anything to screen

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Diagram — Top: CPU with a single arrow labeled 'Dispatch(64, 1, 1)' pointing down. Middle: a grid of 64 small boxes (8x8) labeled 'Thread Groups' with each containing even smaller boxes labeled 'Threads'. Bottom: a texture/buffer labeled 'Output'. Arrows from threads to output labeled 'Write results'. Use a data-center/grid visual with blue processing nodes.
Compute Shader Anatomy

Unlike vertex/fragment shaders, compute shaders use a `.compute` file extension and declare a `[numthreads(x,y,z)]` attribute. They're dispatched from C# using `ComputeShader.Dispatch()` with a 3D grid of thread groups.

blocks.output: Procedural animated pattern written to a texture by the GPU

blocks.value: Dispatching from C#
Compute shaders are controlled entirely from C# scripts. You create a RenderTexture, set it as the compute shader's output, then dispatch the kernel with the right thread group dimensions.

blocks.output: Animated procedural texture displayed on a quad in the scene

blocks.value: GPU Particle Systems

One of the most powerful compute shader applications is GPU particle simulation. Instead of updating thousands of particles on the CPU (slow), you run a compute shader that updates positions, velocities, and lifetimes in parallel on the GPU.

blocks.alt: Visual showing thousands of GPU particles: flocking birds, flowing water, or swirling magic particles
blocks.caption: GPU particles can simulate millions of elements in real-time

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot — A dramatic scene with thousands of glowing particles forming a spiral or fountain pattern. Show a small UI overlay: 'Particles: 1,000,000' and 'FPS: 60'. Use a magical or sci-fi theme with bright particle trails against a dark background. Include a tiny inset showing the compute shader code concept.

blocks.output: 1,000,000+ particles simulated entirely on GPU at 60 FPS

blocks.value: Compute Shaders vs Vertex/Fragment Shaders

Compute shaders free you from the vertex→fragment pipeline. You can write to any buffer, read from any texture, and structure your threads however you need. But they can't render directly to screen — you must write to a texture or buffer that a regular shader then displays.

blocks.question: What file extension do compute shaders use in Unity?
blocks.explanation: Compute shaders in Unity use the .compute extension. Regular shaders use .shader, and include files use .hlsl or .cginc.

blocks.question: What C# method launches a compute shader kernel?
blocks.explanation: Dispatch() launches the compute kernel with a specified number of thread groups in X, Y, and Z dimensions. Each group contains the threads defined by [numthreads].

blocks.question: What attribute declares how many threads run in each thread group?
blocks.explanation: [numthreads(8, 8, 1)] declares 64 threads per group (8×8×1). The total threads dispatched = numthreads × Dispatch() arguments.

blocks.value: Fullscreen Effects for the Entire Scene

Post-processing shaders run on the entire rendered scene after all objects are drawn. They're how games achieve film-like color grading, bloom, motion blur, vignette, and screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO). In URP, you create these as custom Renderer Features or fullscreen shader passes.

blocks.alt: Before/after comparison: raw game scene vs same scene with post-processing (bloom, color grading, vignette)
blocks.caption: Post-processing transforms a raw render into a cinematic final image

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Before/After Split — Left: a raw 3D scene (flat lighting, washed-out colors, no atmosphere). Right: same scene with post-processing applied — warm color grading, subtle bloom on bright areas, dark vignette at edges, slight chromatic aberration. Label 'Raw Render' vs 'With Post-Processing'. Use a fantasy or sci-fi environment for visual impact.
Fullscreen Shader Setup in URP

A fullscreen shader in URP uses a special vertex shader that generates a full-screen triangle without any mesh data. The fragment shader then samples the `_CameraOpaqueTexture` (the rendered scene) and applies effects.

blocks.output: Scene with darkened edges that fade toward the center

blocks.value: Chromatic Aberration Effect

Chromatic aberration simulates lens distortion by offsetting the red, green, and blue channels differently at screen edges. It's a subtle but effective cinematic touch used in games like Resident Evil and Cyberpunk 2077.

blocks.alt: Close-up showing RGB channel separation at screen edges creating chromatic aberration
blocks.caption: Chromatic aberration offsets RGB channels at screen edges for a lens-distortion look

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Close-up Detail — A zoomed-in corner of a screen showing the RGB channel separation. The red channel is shifted outward (away from center), blue shifted inward (toward center), green stays centered. Show a thin white line or high-contrast edge to make the separation visible. Label 'R', 'G', 'B' with small arrows showing shift directions. Use a dark scene with bright neon edges for maximum effect.

blocks.output: RGB color fringing at screen edges, stronger at corners

blocks.value: Custom Renderer Feature in URP
To integrate a post-processing shader into URP's render pipeline, you create a custom Renderer Feature. This tells URP when and how to inject your fullscreen pass into the frame rendering.

blocks.output: Post-processing effect automatically applied to the camera every frame

blocks.value: Common Post-Processing Effects Reference

Here are the most common post-processing effects and their core techniques:
• **Vignette** — darken screen edges based on distance from center
• **Bloom** — blur bright areas and add them back (requires multi-pass blur)
• **Color Grading** — apply LUT (Look-Up Texture) or matrix transform to colors
• **Chromatic Aberration** — offset RGB channels at edges
• **Film Grain** — add noise based on screen UV + time
• **Scanlines** — horizontal lines based on screen Y position
• **Night Vision** — green tint + noise + vignette + light amplification

blocks.question: What is the special vertex shader technique for fullscreen shaders that requires no mesh?
blocks.explanation: Using SV_VertexID to generate a single large triangle that covers the screen is more efficient than a quad (2 triangles) because it eliminates the diagonal edge and requires no mesh data at all.

blocks.question: What URP class do you inherit from to create a custom post-processing pass?
blocks.explanation: You create a class inheriting from ScriptableRenderPass and override Execute() to inject your fullscreen blit into URP's rendering pipeline.

blocks.question: What function samples the rendered scene color in a fullscreen post-processing shader?
blocks.explanation: SampleSceneColor(uv) reads from the _CameraOpaqueTexture, which contains the color of the scene before post-processing. It's available when including DeclareOpaqueTexture.hlsl.

parts.partTitle: Part 15: Capstone Project — Stylized Water Shader

blocks.value: Build Your First Production Shader

Congratulations — you've learned all the fundamentals! Now let's put everything together in a Stylized Water Shader. This project uses: vertex displacement, normal mapping, depth-based foam, color gradients, specular highlights, and transparency. It's a complete, portfolio-ready shader that demonstrates mastery of every concept in this course.

blocks.alt: Mind map showing all concepts connected to the water shader project: vertex displacement, normals, depth, color, specular, transparency
blocks.caption: This project ties together every concept you've learned in the course

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Mind Map/Concept Map — Central node 'Stylized Water Shader' with 6 branches: 'Vertex Displacement' (waves), 'Normal Mapping' (surface detail), 'Depth-Based Foam' (screen-space), 'Color Gradient' (deep vs shallow), 'Specular Highlights' (sun reflection), 'Transparency & Refraction' (see-through water). Each branch has a small icon and connects to the central water drop icon. Use ocean blue/teal colors.
Project Requirements

Your water shader should:
1. **Vertex waves** — animate the mesh surface with sine waves in the vertex shader
2. **Normal mapping** — add surface detail with scrolling normal maps
3. **Depth-based foam** — white foam where water intersects geometry (screen-space)
4. **Color gradient** — deep blue in the center, turquoise at edges
5. **Specular highlights** — Blinn-Phong sun reflection on wave peaks
6. **Transparency** — see through to the underwater floor with refraction distortion
7. **Properties** — expose wave speed, height, color, foam width, and normal strength in the Inspector

blocks.alt: Final water shader result: stylized ocean with waves, foam at shore, specular sun reflection, and visible underwater floor
blocks.caption: Your finished water shader will look like this in the Unity scene

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot — A beautiful stylized water scene in Unity. A large plane with animated waves (not flat — actual vertex displacement). White foam lines where water meets a sandy shore. Bright specular highlight from a directional sun. Turquoise-to-deep-blue color gradient. Slight transparency showing underwater sand texture with refraction distortion. Include a small inset of the Material Inspector showing the tweakable properties. Use a bright, cheerful daytime scene.

blocks.output: Animated stylized water with waves, foam, specular highlights, and depth-based color

blocks.value: Code Structure Tips

As your shaders grow, organization matters. Follow these patterns:
• Group related properties with `[Header()]` attributes
• Define all properties at the top of HLSLPROGRAM
• Keep vertex and fragment functions focused — one main task each
• Use clear struct names (Attributes/Varyings is the URP standard)
• Comment each major section (waves, normals, foam, lighting, combine)
• Separate reusable logic into #include files for other shaders
Testing Your Water Shader

Before declaring your project done, test these scenarios:
• **Wave animation** — waves move smoothly without popping or jitter
• **Foam at shore** — foam appears where water meets land/rocks
• **Foam width** — adjusting _FoamWidth property changes foam spread
• **Deep vs shallow color** — color changes based on water depth
• **Specular angle** — highlight moves correctly as you orbit the camera
• **Normal strength** — surface detail increases/decreases with property
• **Transparency** — underwater objects visible through the water
• **Performance** — maintains 60 FPS with the water plane in view
Common Beginner Mistakes

Watch out for these pitfalls when building your water shader:
• **Forgetting ZWrite Off** for transparent shaders — causes sorting artifacts
• **Wrong depth comparison** — remember sceneDepth > waterDepth means floor is BEHIND water
• **Missing normalize()** on interpolated normals — causes lighting to look wrong at grazing angles
• **Not reconstructing Z** after scaling normal XY — breaks unit-length vectors
• **Forgetting ComputeScreenPos()** in vertex shader — screen UVs will be wrong
• **Using linear depth incorrectly** — always convert with LinearEyeDepth() before comparing
• **Wave frequency too high** — causes vertex popping and aliasing
What You Practiced

**Vertex displacement** — animate mesh geometry with sine waves
**Normal mapping** — scrolling normals with TBN transformation
**Screen-space depth** — foam based on scene depth buffer
**Color blending** — lerp between shallow and deep colors
**Specular lighting** — Blinn-Phong highlights on wave peaks
**Transparency** — alpha blending with ZWrite Off
**Material properties** — artist-friendly Inspector controls
**URP integration** — proper includes, structs, and helper functions
Challenge: Extend Your Water Shader

Try adding these features on your own:
• **Refraction** — distort underwater view using normal maps and `SampleSceneColor`
• **Caustics** — animated light patterns on the underwater floor
• **Foam noise** — use a noise texture to make foam edges irregular and organic
• **Multiple wave layers** — combine 3-4 sine waves at different frequencies for more natural motion
• **Edge detection** — sharper foam where water meets vertical walls
• **Reflection probe support** — add sky/environment reflections
• **Gerstner waves** — more realistic wave math used in professional water systems
• **Underwater fog** — color shift when camera is below the water surface

blocks.alt: Roadmap showing beginner water shader → intermediate features → advanced ocean system
blocks.caption: Your journey doesn't end here — keep building on this foundation

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Roadmap/Progression Illustration — A winding path or staircase going upward over stylized waves. Step 1: 'Basic Water' (current project, green checkmark). Step 2: 'Refraction + Caustics' (yellow, in progress). Step 3: 'Gerstner Waves' (blue, future). Step 4: 'Full Ocean System' (purple, advanced). Each step has a small water-themed icon. Motivational, encouraging style with ocean colors.
Where to Go Next

You've completed the HLSL Shader Programming course! Here's your learning path forward:
• **Advanced Lighting** — PBR (Physically Based Rendering), image-based lighting, area lights
• **Tessellation Shaders** — GPU geometry subdivision for displacement mapping
• **Geometry Shaders** — generate new primitives (grass, fur, particle trails)
• **Ray Marching** — volumetric fog, clouds, and signed distance fields
• **Deferred Rendering** — work with G-buffers for advanced lighting
• **Custom SRP** — build your own render pipeline from scratch
• **Portfolio Projects** — toon ocean, holographic UI, magical effects, procedural terrain

blocks.question: Which technique creates white foam where water intersects with underwater geometry?
blocks.explanation: By comparing the water's depth with the scene depth behind it, we detect where water is close to geometry and add foam. This is the standard technique for shoreline foam in water shaders.

blocks.question: Why must ZWrite be Off for transparent water shaders?
options: It makes the shader compile faster
Transparent objects writing depth causes sorting artifacts
blocks.correctAnswer: Transparent objects writing depth causes sorting artifacts
blocks.explanation: If transparent objects write to the depth buffer, objects behind them may be incorrectly culled, causing visual glitches. Transparent objects should only read depth (ZTest LEqual), not write it.

blocks.question: What URP function computes screen-space position from clip-space position for depth sampling?
blocks.explanation: ComputeScreenPos(clipPosition) returns a float4 where .xy/.w gives normalized screen UVs needed for SampleSceneDepth(). It must be called in the vertex shader and divided by .w in the fragment shader.
